results.evidence: Three row fields say Grade III and the commitment chip says II. The 2004 AAJ account of the Southern Picket Enchainment gives Frenzlespitz as "II 5.6", which supports the outlier rather than the majority; no second source for either numeral was found, so nothing is changed.

results.correct_value: From the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, descend roughly 500 ft on the north side (below Ottohorn's north face) to the foot of Frenzel Spitz's south face, then climb it; no crest traverse over Ottohorn.
results.evidence: The 1962 AAJ first-ascent account says Frenzelspitz sits off the main chain close under the north face of Ottohorn and that the party had to descend about 500 ft of that face to gain access. A 2011 enchainment report describes rappelling the broken couloir and glacier off the north side of the Himmelhorn/Ottohorn col to reach the south face of Frenzelspitz. Both agree with the approach text and summit directions; the itinerary day 3, summit note, col note, pro_needs and overview were the outliers.

results.fact: Which side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col leads to Frenzel Spitz / back to camp
results.correct_value: The south (Crescent Creek) side is the way up from and back to camp; the north side (broken couloir, glacier and moats, usually rappelled) is the way down to Frenzel Spitz.
results.evidence: The first-ascent account places Frenzelspitz below Ottohorn's north face and reached by a 500 ft descent of that face; a 2011 report rappelled the couloir and glacier off the north side of the col to reach Frenzelspitz's south face. A Pickets reference page confirms the north side of the col is loose, tricky 5th class and the south side is friendlier. So the base-finding claim that the north side leads away from Frenzel Spitz is wrong, and descent_text wrongly routed the return to Crescent Creek Basin down the north side.

patches.find: If the ground below you needs a rope to descend, you are on the north side and you are heading for the Mustard Glacier, not Frenzel Spitz.
patches.replace: That north side is the way to Frenzel Spitz, which sits under Ottohorn's north face: the 500 ft descent to the route's base goes down it, and the friendly Crescent Creek side is only the way up to the col and back to camp.

results.evidence: The two claims describe different places (summit gully vs the step below the col), so they are not strictly incompatible, but the RAPPELS text never mentions the col rappel and its summit-gully raps, 70 m option and "Crossover Descent" could not be confirmed by any source. The only sourced rappel is off the north side of the Otto-Himmel col (2011 report). No patch without a second source.

Sources genuinely vary: a Pickets reference calls both Barrier crossings "classic Pickets Class 3" (loose, can be death-defying when wet); other reports call it "serious Class 3" or describe crossing a moat onto low-fifth-class terrain. No two sources agree on a single rating, so the row's 3rd/4th/low-5th spread is left as is.

Parties camp on several benches: one description keeps to the ~5,800 ft band, another reports a flat area below Mount Terror at about 6,050 ft. No two sources agree on one camp elevation, so 5,900 / 6,050 / 6,200 are left unchanged.

results.correct_value: The rock climb is not glaciated, but the approach below the north side of the col crosses glacier and moat terrain.

Only the avalanche panel label "non-glaciated" disagreed.

results.correct_value: Terror Basin and Crescent Creek are walk-up-only cross-country zones (not reservable in advance); the permit is issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day of or the day before the trip.
results.evidence: The park's backcountry-reservations page says only Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price, Triumph and Tapto Lakes cross-country zones can be reserved and the rest are walk-up only; the park's cross-country zone table lists both Terror Basin and Crescent Creek as walk-up only, 6 per party. The permits page says walk-up permits are issued the day of or day before, most must be picked up in person, and email walk-up permits apply only to other trailheads (Baker Lake, Mt Baker Hwy, Twisp); an independent permit guide agrees most walk-up sites need in-person pickup.
